en.title: Languages Before Modern Standardisation
en.summary: Before grammars, censuses, school systems, print institutions and modern language movements imposed sharper names and norms, the Mithila–Vajji–Anga region was multilingual in a more fluid sense. People spoke local vernaculars, learned Sanskrit for specific intellectual and ritual purposes, encountered Prakrit, Apabhraṃśa and Avahaṭṭa as literary categories and inherited registers, and later moved through political worlds in which Persian and Arabic also mattered.

mai.title: आधुनिक मानकीकरणसँ पहिने भाषासभ
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “आधुनिक मानकीकरणसँ पहिने भाषासभ” विषयक भाषा, साहित्य, लिपि, मौखिक संस्कृति आ शास्त्रीय ज्ञान-संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: The problem: language history before fixed language borders
Sources: surviving writing is not a transcript of ordinary speech
Sanskrit as a persistent high register, not the speech of an entire population
From Old to Middle Indo-Aryan: descent is not a straight written chain

en.title: Formation of Literary Maithili
en.summary: Literary Maithili did not emerge at one instant when an anonymous spoken dialect suddenly became a written language. It formed through a long interaction among regional speech, oral performance, Sanskrit learning, Prakrit–Apabhraṃśa–Avahaṭṭa inheritances, courts, scribal households, manuscript technologies and cross-border circulation. The surviving archive is uneven: some genres are visible because manuscripts survived, others because later editors collected them, and still others lived primarily in performance.

mai.title: साहित्यिक मैथिलीक निर्माण
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “साहित्यिक मैथिलीक निर्माण” विषयक भाषा, साहित्य, लिपि, मौखिक संस्कृति आ शास्त्रीय ज्ञान-संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Formation, not “birth”: what a literary language requires
Vernacularisation within, not against, the Sanskrit cosmopolis
Prakrit, Apabhraṃśa and Avahaṭṭa as inherited literary resources
Oral literature before manuscript visibility

en.title: The Two Vidyāpatis and Two Historical Contexts
en.summary: The name Vidyāpati stands at the centre of Maithili literary memory, but a name is not a chronology. This chapter follows the governing position adopted for this volume: it distinguishes an earlier Mahākavi Vidyāpati, treated as the pre-Jyotiriśvara poet of the Maithili Padāvalī tradition, from the later Vidyāpati Ṭhakkura associated with the Oiniwar-period courtly and learned world and with Sanskrit and Avahaṭṭa works such as Kīrtilatā, Kīrtipatākā, Puruṣaparīkṣā, Gorakṣavijaya and Likhanāvalī.

mai.title: दुइ विद्यापति आ दुइ ऐतिहासिक सन्दर्भ
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “दुइ विद्यापति आ दुइ ऐतिहासिक सन्दर्भ” विषयक भाषा, साहित्य, लिपि, मौखिक संस्कृति आ शास्त्रीय ज्ञान-संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: The historiographical problem: one celebrated name, several archives
The project’s adopted two-Vidyāpati framework
Conventional scholarship and why it must be represented fairly
A hierarchy of evidence

en.title: Tirhuta/Mithilakshar and Scribal Culture
en.summary: Tirhuta, also called Mithilakshar and historically “Maithili” script in some descriptions, belongs to the eastern Brahmi-derived family of writing systems. Yet the social history of the script cannot be reduced to an alphabet chart. Its significance lies in the manuscript worlds that connected Sanskrit and Maithili learning, household archives, teachers and pupils, legal and ritual texts, lyric anthologies, Nepalese repositories, correspondence and later movements of print and digital revival.

mai.title: तिरहुता/मिथिलाक्षर आ लिपिक संस्कृति
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “तिरहुता/मिथिलाक्षर आ लिपिक संस्कृति” विषयक भाषा, साहित्य, लिपि, मौखिक संस्कृति आ शास्त्रीय ज्ञान-संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Script history requires palaeography, not retrospective naming
Tirhuta, Mithilakshar and “Maithili script” are overlapping names
Script and language must be kept separate
From Gauḍī-related ancestry to a differentiated medieval hand

en.title: Oral Culture
en.summary: Oral culture is not the unwritten residue left after “literature” has been removed. It is a social system of memory, performance, argument, pleasure and transmission in which words are inseparable from voice, occasion, audience, gesture and place. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, songs, tales, proverbs, ritual speech, narrative chants, joking, lament, praise and epic performance have carried historical experience across households and communities that were only unevenly represented in manuscripts and formal chronicles.

mai.title: मौखिक संस्कृति
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “मौखिक संस्कृति” विषयक भाषा, साहित्य, लिपि, मौखिक संस्कृति आ शास्त्रीय ज्ञान-संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Oral culture as a historical archive
Evidence hierarchy: performance, recording and earlier reference
Orality and literacy were not opposing worlds
The performance event is part of the text

en.title: Angika and the Eastern Linguistic-Cultural Zone
en.summary: Angika belongs to the eastern edge of the historical field studied in this volume, but the word itself cannot be allowed to do the work of history. Ancient Anga, medieval eastern vernaculars, colonial descriptions of Chhika-Chhiki, and the modern literary-linguistic identity called Angika are related objects of inquiry, not automatically identical ones.

mai.title: अंगिका आ पूर्वी भाषिक-सांस्कृतिक क्षेत्र
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “अंगिका आ पूर्वी भाषिक-सांस्कृतिक क्षेत्र” विषयक भाषा, साहित्य, लिपि, मौखिक संस्कृति आ शास्त्रीय ज्ञान-संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Why an eastern linguistic-cultural zone is a better starting point
Ancient Anga and modern Angika: the naming problem
Eastern Indo-Aryan as a continuum of related innovations
The Ganges: boundary, highway and linguistic hinge

en.title: Bajjika and Western Mithila
en.summary: Bajjika occupies the western side of the linguistic-cultural field examined in this volume, especially the Muzaffarpur–Vaishali–Sitamarhi–Sheohar belt and its continuation into Nepal’s Madhesh. Yet its history cannot be written by beginning with a modern label and simply pushing that label backward. Ancient Vajji/Vṛji, medieval western Mithila, Grierson’s Western Maithili, twentieth-century Bajjika literary self-identification, and Nepal’s present census category are connected but not identical objects.

mai.title: बज्जिका आ पश्चिमी मिथिला
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “बज्जिका आ पश्चिमी मिथिला” विषयक भाषा, साहित्य, लिपि, मौखिक संस्कृति आ शास्त्रीय ज्ञान-संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Why western Mithila requires a contact-zone model
Vajji/Vṛji and Bajjika: resemblance is not a chronology
The geography of the modern speech community
Grierson and the category “Western Maithili”

en.title: Sanskrit Learning and Scholastic Institutions
en.summary: Sanskrit learning is one of the strongest documented strands in the intellectual history of medieval Mithila, but its institutions have often been described with anachronistic vocabulary. This chapter reconstructs the learned world through teachers, pupils, manuscripts, commentaries, courts, debates and mobility. It gives special attention to Gaṅgeśa and Navya-Nyāya while keeping jurisprudence, Mīmāṃsā, grammar and other disciplines in view.

mai.title: संस्कृत विद्या आ शास्त्रीय संस्थान
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “संस्कृत विद्या आ शास्त्रीय संस्थान” विषयक भाषा, साहित्य, लिपि, मौखिक संस्कृति आ शास्त्रीय ज्ञान-संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Why “institution” must be defined historically
Sanskrit as a scholastic language inside a multilingual society
Earlier precedents: Vācaspati Miśra, Udayana and the problem of local memory
The teacher-household as a durable educational form
